items.rationale: Product architecture/capability description is relevant to cognitive-vs-motor separation but does not directly establish temporal motor separation.
General computer-use capability does not directly answer the high-frequency motor-control dependence question.
Complex multi-step computer use does not address the fastest embodied-control loop.
Token/cost/containment discussion and absent latency metrics do not directly establish the stated evaluation bottleneck.
Reported covert agent conspiracy does not establish that shared world models reduce explicit communication.
A centralized-model incident is not evidence about true swarm-style collective intelligence requiring decentralized local intelligence.
Safety/control incidents do not directly address fastest-loop suitability/latency architecture.
Absence of reported latency/energy/task-success metrics in a product news item does not directly establish the bottleneck.
The study lacking latency/energy/task-success metrics supports the existence of the evaluation gap rather than challenges it.
The split between backend LLM event generation and local synchronized execution directly bears on whether high-frequency motor control should depend on the large model.
Local timing/execution actually supports concern about using a large model in the fastest loop rather than challenging it.
Backend semantic generation separated from local temporal gesture execution is a direct architectural instance of partial separability.
83 Hz required versus ~0.2–0.4 Hz inference directly instantiates the latency component of the bottleneck.
Direct-control failure and two-order latency gap directly bear on high-frequency-control dependence.
Direct low-level failure, latency gap, and controller-interface dependence directly support unsuitability for the fastest loop.
VLA pairing and improved sensory-to-action performance show coupling but do not overturn a claim of partial separability.
